summary.en: Colombia has opened an embassy in Jerusalem and launched a cultural counterrevolution that is removing more than thirty artworks from the National Museum and ordering the removal of LGBTQ2S+ political works. The Mobile Anti-Riot Squad (ESMAD) has returned to operate in the country and an evangelist was killed after refusing to lend a motorcycle to a criminal group in Cartagena. Former rebel leaders have been charged with war crimes against Indigenous groups, while the president has called for US troops on the ground and linked Colombia's peace process to democratic change in Venezuela. An earthquake in Colombia has left more than 224 dead and rescue operations continue, and a Colombian asylum seeker was tackled by ICE agents outside his home in Washington. 225 battle-related deaths were recorded in 2024, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Colombia har åpnet en ambassade i Jerusalem og igangsatt en kulturell motrevolusjon som fjerner mer enn tretti kunstverk fra Nasjonalmuseet og har beordret fjerning av LGBTQ2S+-politiske verk. Den mobile antiopprørsgruppen (ESMAD) har vendt tilbake til å operere i landet, og en evangelisk predikant ble drept etter å ha nektet å låne en motorsykkel til en kriminell gruppe i Cartagena. Tidligere opprørsledere er blitt siktet for krigsforbrytelser mot urfolk, mens presidenten har oppfordret til amerikanske soldater på bakken og knyttet Colombias fredsprosess til demokratisk endring i Venezuela. Et jordskjelv i Colombia har etterlatt mer enn 224 døde, og redningsarbeidet pågår, og en colombiansk asylsøker ble taklet av ICE-agenter utenfor hjemmet sitt i Washington. 225 dødsfall knyttet til kamper ble registrert i 2024, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Colombian conflict
background.extract: The Colombian conflict began on May 27, 1964, and is a low-intensity asymmetric war between the government of Colombia, paramilitary groups, crime syndicates, and far-left guerrilla groups engaged in armed factional hostilities to increase their influence in Colombian territory. Some of the most important international contributors to the Colombian conflict include multinational corporations, the United States, Cuba, and the drug trafficking industry.
